description:
We are SUTian’s, a team of technology enthusiasts passionate about software engineering, innovation, and space exploration. Our goal is to develop reliable and innovative solutions that contribute to astronaut health, safety, and well-being during long-duration space missions.

For this challenge, we aim to create an intelligent health-monitoring solution capable of tracking astronauts’ vital signs, identifying potential health anomalies, and providing useful insights to support crew safety.
summary: COSMO is a voice-first AI health companion that lives in an astronaut’s wrist device and projects a holographic screen. On long missions, crews are far from Earth, communication is delayed, and there is no doctor on board. COSMO reads data from a wearable band and smart shirt, learns what “normal” looks like for one specific astronaut, and notices when their readings drift away from it, often before they feel anything. It then talks with them out loud: it asks how they feel, checks their readings, walks them through approved self-care steps taken from NASA’s own countermeasure lists, rechecks, and logs everything for the flight surgeon.  COSMO covers both physical and mental health. It explores feelings before suggesting anything, remembers what helps each astronaut, has a real sense of humor, and switches to simple yes/no questions when an astronaut is alone in an emergency. Medical decisions always come from a fixed, reviewable rulebook, never from the AI, so the system stays safe and predictable while still feeling like a crewmate you can talk to about anything.  Our working prototype is a website that simulates the full device using real research data (NASA’s Inspiration4 lab data and physiological recordings from PhysioNet), a 3D holographic body, live voice conversation, and an AI language model.
details:
COSMO — Your Companion Beyond Earth

What does it do and how does it work?

COSMO is an AI-powered health and wellbeing companion designed to support astronauts during long-duration space missions. It monitors vital signs, learns each astronaut's personal health baseline, detects unusual deviations, and interacts with astronauts through natural voice conversations.

COSMO works through three layers:

  1. Health Monitoring and Learning: It processes heart rate, HRV, blood oxygen, breathing rate, skin temperature, stress index, and activity data. It builds an individual baseline for each astronaut and detects unusual changes relative to their normal patterns. Baseline learning pauses when readings appear abnormal to prevent unusual conditions from becoming the new normal.
  2. Safety and Decision Layer: A deterministic rule engine evaluates health deviations and reported symptoms, identifies conditions requiring attention, and provides predefined response steps informed by NASA Human Research Program research. Medical workflows are controlled by predefined rules, not generated by AI.
  3. AI Companion: Astronauts can communicate with COSMO using voice through the wake phrase "Hey COSMO". A dialogue manager handles safety-critical interactions, while Google Gemini 2.5 Flash handles general conversation, contextual questions, and emotional support. COSMO also remembers permitted personal preferences and previous helpful activities to make interactions more personalized.

The platform demonstrates these capabilities through an interactive 3D human body, live health dashboards, proactive alerts, voice conversations, mental wellness check-ins, simulated medical scenarios, and a mission log with an Earth communication and synchronization queue.

What benefits does it have?

COSMO offers several benefits:

  • Detects unusual health changes using individual baselines rather than relying exclusively on population averages.
  • Provides consistent initial guidance without requiring immediate communication with Earth.
  • Supports psychological wellbeing through personalized conversations, voluntary check-ins, relaxation activities, and emotional support.
  • Maintains a record of relevant health events for review by flight surgeons.
  • Supports continued local monitoring and event logging during communication interruptions.

What is the intended impact of the project?

COSMO aims to improve astronaut health awareness and psychological wellbeing during long-duration missions to the Moon, Mars, and beyond. By combining personalized monitoring, structured safety workflows, and AI companionship, it explores how astronauts could receive continuous support despite communication delays and isolation from Earth. Its long-term approach could also benefit people working in other isolated environments, such as submarines, remote research stations, and distant medical facilities.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Frontend: Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS.
  • 3D visualization: Three.js and React Three Fiber.
  • Data visualization: Recharts.
  • Voice interaction: Web Speech API for speech recognition and synthesis.
  • AI language model: Google Gemini 2.5 Flash through OpenRouter.
  • Backend and data processing: Node.js scripts.
  • Deployment: Vercel.
  • Testing: 210 automated tests covering dialogue and safety workflows.
  • Research: NASA Human Research Program resources and space-health research recordings.

The current prototype uses simulated sensor readings and replayed research recordings. No physical wearable devices or spacecraft hardware are connected.

How is your project creative?

COSMO combines personalized health monitoring, proactive voice interaction, mental wellness support, and 3D health visualization in one astronaut-facing companion. Its most distinctive feature is the separation between conversational AI and safety-critical decisions: a controlled rule engine manages predefined medical workflows, while the language model provides natural conversation without being allowed to override safety procedures.

COSMO also learns individual health patterns, initiates check-ins when unusual changes occur, and uses personal context to make its support more meaningful. This transforms the traditional health-monitoring dashboard into an interactive companion designed around both the physical and psychological challenges of spaceflight.

What factors did your team consider?

Our team considered:

  • Astronaut safety and the need for medically reviewed response protocols.
  • Individual physiological differences and the importance of personal baselines.
  • Psychological challenges such as isolation, confinement, stress, and disrupted sleep.
  • Communication delays and the need for local operation when Earth is unavailable.
  • Privacy and protection of personal health and emotional information.
  • Ease of use during stressful or demanding mission conditions.
  • Hardware, computing, and connectivity limitations in spacecraft.
  • Scientific reliability and the distinction between simulated data, research findings, and clinically validated medical procedures.

COSMO is currently a research prototype, and its illustrative medical protocols require review by qualified medical professionals before operational use.
